Q: WSO2 APIM 4.4.0 Operation Policy Issue A:

This is a gap in how WSO2 APIM handles Operation Policy sequences versus regular API synapse artifacts in distributed deployments. The root cause is architectural, policy sequences follow a different packaging and sync path than the API synapse XML, and several things must be correctly wired for them to land on the Gateway.

In a distributed setup, the policy's .j2 template is rendered into a sequence and that sequence needs to be included inside the API's synapse artifact bundle when the Gateway pulls it at deploy time. If any step in this chain is broken, the API XML deploys fine (endpoints work) but the policy sequence is not their causing the exact Sequence: {policy_name} not found error you're seeing while the backend still receives the request.

Q: Running purrr functionals in parallel: imap A:

Over in Futureverse, you can use the new futurize package and its futurize() function - it allows you to keep your original code as-is. It works with purrr and tons of other types of calls.

In your case, use:

library(futurize)
plan(multisession)
...
d1 <- imap(sampled_ids, resamp_df, df) |> futurize()

That's it!

PS. If you prefer non-pipe syntax, you can use d1 <- futurize(imap(sampled_ids, resamp_df, df)), which is an identical call.

Details

Say you use:

library(purrr)
z <- imap(5:8, ~ runif(.y, max = .x))

You can parallelize this by piping the expression to futurize() as in:

library(purrr)

## Set up parallel workers
library(futurize)
plan(multisession)

z <- imap(5:8, ~ runif(.y, max = .x)) |> futurize(seed = TRUE)

Here we use seed = TRUE to tell futureverse to set up proper parallel RNG. If there are no random number generated, it's just ... |> futurize().

You've got several other backends to choose from, e.g. plan(future.mirai::mirai_multisession).

Q: Always best to use float in python script instead of int? A:

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 gives False - and this is main problem with float

If you convert it to strings with more decimal places then you get

>>> print(f"{0.3:.54f}")
0.299999999999999988897769753748434595763683319091796875
>>> print(f"{0.1+0.2:.54f}")
0.300000000000000044408920985006261616945266723632812500

Python doc: 15. Floating-Point Arithmetic: Issues and Limitations

See also page: 0.30000000000000004.com

Q: Why does our website load fast on USA but load slow while accessing site from India? A:

This mainly happens due to server connection. If you host it using a particular server region and try to access it from another region it will take time to load.
